## How Is Orthopedic Medical Coding Different from Any Other Specialty Coding


[Orthopedic medical coding](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/ai-orthopedic-medical-coding) follows the same basic process as other specialties. Coders review clinical documentation, assign ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes and CPT/HCPCS procedure codes, apply modifiers, and validate claims against applicable billing requirements.


However, orthopedic coding requires greater attention to anatomical details, surgical techniques, laterality, and procedure-specific reimbursement rules. A 2025 study found that at least[four of five orthopedic surgeons](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12063514/) agreed on the primary CPT code in only 33.3% of cases, and on modifier usage in just 41.7%. This highlights the complexity of orthopedic coding, even among experienced surgeons.


Hospitals face additional complexity because inpatient facility procedures use ICD-10-PCS, while physician professional services generally use CPT/HCPCS.


## 6 Major Medical Coding Challenges in Orthopedic Practices


### 1. Different Payers Require Different Modifiers for the Same Procedure


One of the biggest orthopedic coding challenges is that insurers may require different modifiers and claim formats for the same procedure. Coders must account for laterality, procedure-specific rules, and payer requirements to avoid denials and underpayments.


> For example, consider a patient undergoing the same eligible procedure on both knees during one surgical session. Depending on the payer's requirements:
>
>
> Modifier 50 may be required to report the bilateral procedure on one claim line.
> Modifiers RT and LT may be required on separate lines to identify procedures performed on the right and left knees.


According to CMS,[Medicare](https://www.cms.gov/help/status-indicators) generally reimburses eligible bilateral procedures with payment indicator 1 at **150% of the single-procedure fee schedule amount** , subject to applicable payment rules. However, commercial insurers and Medicaid programs may follow different billing conventions.


The challenge isn't necessarily frequent changes in payer policies, but consistently applying the correct rules across insurers. Using the wrong modifier or claim format can delay or reduce reimbursement, even when the underlying[orthopedic CPT code](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/orthopedic-cpt-codes) is correct.

It applies each payer's modifier and laterality conventions automatically — modifier 50 for a bilateral procedure on one payer, RT/LT on separate lines for another — and validates the finished claim against that payer's rules before submission, so the correct format reaches the payer even when the CPT code is identical across insurers.


### 2. Prior Authorization Details Don't Always Match the Final Procedure


[Orthopedic surgeries](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/icd-10-codes-for-orthopedic-surgery) often require prior authorization, but the approved services may not always match the procedures ultimately performed. Discrepancies in CPT codes, laterality, or authorization details can lead to denials, even when the medical coding is accurate.


For example, a surgeon receives authorization for a knee procedure but performs an additional procedure after identifying another problem during surgery. Before billing, the practice must verify whether the additional service requires separate authorization or qualifies for retrospective approval.


Other common discrepancies include:


- **Incorrect CPT code or laterality:** The authorization doesn't match the procedure or surgical site.
- **Date mismatch:** The procedure falls outside the authorization's approved date range.
- **Missing procedure approval:** Additional services performed aren't covered by the original authorization.


The administrative burden is significant. According to the[AMA's 2025 prior authorization survey](https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf) , practices completed an average of **39 prior authorizations per physician per week** , consuming approximately 13 hours of physician and staff time.


For orthopedic practices, this makes authorization verification an essential pre-bill step. Coding and billing teams must ensure that the procedures documented, coded, and submitted align with the payer's authorization requirements.

### 3. Multiple Orthopedic Procedures Create Bundling and Unbundling Risks


Orthopedic surgeries often involve several related procedures during the same operative session.


For example, a surgeon performing knee arthroscopy might repair a meniscus and perform debridement.


The coder must determine whether the debridement is separately reportable or included in another billed procedure. This depends on the specific CPT codes, operative documentation, applicable NCCI edits, and payer policies.


Two types of errors can occur:


**Unbundling:** Billing procedures separately when they should be included in a comprehensive procedure code.


**Undercoding:** Failing to report a distinct, separately payable procedure supported by documentation and coding rules.


Both affect revenue integrity. Unbundling creates compliance and denial risks, while[undercoding](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/ai-medical-coding-audit-uncovers-undercoding) can result in missed reimbursement.

It checks code combinations against NCCI edits and payer policy to flag unbundling risk, and — because it reads the complete operative report rather than a charge summary — it catches the separately payable work that otherwise gets undercoded. In a[400-bed deployment](https://www.combinehealth.ai/resources/customer-success-stories/case-study/ai-matched-expert-coders) , that full-record review surfaced 5× more documentation and coding opportunities than the manual workflow.


### 4. Incomplete Documentation Makes Accurate Code Selection Difficult


[Orthopedic medical coding](https://www.combinehealth.ai/specialities/orthopedics-coding-billing) requires detailed documentation of anatomy, injury severity, and procedures performed. Missing clinical details can prevent coders from selecting the most specific ICD-10-CM or CPT code, leading to physician queries, coding delays, or less-specific coding where permitted.


For example, fracture coding may require documentation of:


- **Anatomical details:** Exact bone, fracture location, and laterality.
- **Fracture characteristics:** Whether the fracture is displaced or nondisplaced, open or closed.
- **Healing status:** Whether the fracture is healing routinely, experiencing delayed healing, or has developed nonunion.


> Because CombineHealth reviews documentation as it codes, it flags exactly these gaps — missing laterality, fracture characteristics, or healing status — as a[CDI alert or query](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/cdi-query-vs-alert) before the claim is submitted, rather than after a denial. The query goes out with the specific missing detail identified, so coding isn't held waiting on a vague "fracture follow-up" note.


If a physician documents only "fracture follow-up," the coder may not have enough information to assign the appropriate ICD-10-CM code. Similarly, an operative report that doesn't clearly describe the surgical work performed can make CPT selection difficult.


For large orthopedic groups and health systems, variations in documentation across surgeons further increase manual review, physician queries, and coding turnaround times.


### 5. Global Surgical Periods Complicate E/M Billing


Many orthopedic procedures include postoperative care within a global surgical payment package. Routine follow-up visits during this period are generally included in the original procedure's reimbursement, while certain unrelated services may qualify for separate payment.


For example, a patient recovering from right knee replacement visits the same orthopedic surgeon for a new, unrelated shoulder problem. If the physician performs and documents a separately billable[E/M service](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/e-m-coding-guide) , **modifier 24** may be appropriate under Medicare's global surgery rules.


The challenge is distinguishing routine postoperative care from separately billable services. Incorrectly billing included follow-up visits can trigger denials, while overlooking eligible E/M services can result in missed reimbursement.


### 6. Large Orthopedic Groups Struggle to Maintain Coding Consistency


Large orthopedic groups and health systems often have surgeons working across joint replacement, sports medicine, spine, trauma, and other subspecialties. Differences in documentation styles, procedure complexity, and coding practices make it difficult to maintain consistency across locations.


For example, consider an orthopedic group with 30 surgeons across multiple locations. Two surgeons may perform similar procedures but document them differently, requiring coders to interpret each operative report while applying consistent CPT codes, modifiers, and payer-specific rules.


Without standardized coding workflows, similar encounters may be coded inconsistently, increasing manual audits, coding backlogs, and turnaround times as patient volumes grow.

## Why Even a 10% Orthopedic Denial Rate Can Be Costly


Orthopedic practices don't necessarily need unusually high denial rates to experience substantial financial exposure. With high-value procedures such as joint replacements and fracture surgeries, even a small number of denied claims can affect cash flow.


According to[CMS's 2024 Medicare data](https://www.cms.gov/training-education/medicare-learning-networkr-mln/compliance/medicare-provider-compliance-tips/hip-knee-replacement) , major hip and knee replacements and lower-extremity reattachments accounted for **$546.7 million in projected improper payments** , with a 43.6% improper payment rate. Medical necessity issues accounted for 92.8% of these improper payments.


While improper payments aren't the same as claim denials, these figures highlight the financial stakes of orthopedic reimbursement.
